title: For each department, collect the distinct set of cities where its employees are based, producing a `Map<String, Set<String>>`, using `groupingBy` with a `mapping` downstream into `toSet`. Explain how nested collectors compose.
shortTitle: Collect the distinct set of cities per department using groupingBy with mapping to a Set

s1_definition.profdef: `Collectors.mapping(mapper, downstream)` transforms each element before it reaches the downstream collector. Combined as `groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, mapping(Employee::getCity, toSet()))`, it groups by department and, within each group, maps employees to their city and collects the distinct cities into a `Set`.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh sorts employee files into department trays. But he does not want to keep whole files in each tray — he only wants the list of distinct cities. mapping pulls out just the city from each file as it drops into the tray, and the Set makes sure each city is listed once.
s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(dept, mapping(getCity, toSet()))` groups by department and keeps only the distinct cities per group.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Collectors.mapping(mapper, downstream)` transforms each element before it reaches the downstream collector. Combined as `groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, mapping(Employee::getCity, toSet()))`, it groups by department and, within each group, maps employees to their city and collects the distinct cities into a `Set`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh sorts employee files into department trays. But he does not want to keep whole files in each tray — he only wants the list of distinct cities. mapping pulls out just the city from each file as it drops into the tray, and the Set makes sure each city is listed once.

**One line to remember:** `groupingBy(dept, mapping(getCity, toSet()))` groups by department and keeps only the distinct cities per group.

sections.s2_technical:
`mapping(mapper, downstream)` is an adapting collector: it applies the mapper to each element and feeds the result into the downstream collector. On its own it is rarely used, but nested inside groupingBy it is powerful — it changes what gets collected per group. With `toSet()` as the downstream, duplicates collapse, so each department's value is the distinct set of cities.

A worked finance example: `employees.stream().collect(groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, mapping(Employee::getCity, toSet())))` yields `Map<String, Set<String>>` such as Trading mapped to the set of Mumbai and Bangalore. If two Trading employees are both in Mumbai, the Set stores Mumbai once.

The senior nuance is that collectors compose like building blocks: the classifier decides the key, mapping decides what the grouped values are, and the innermost collector decides how they are gathered — toList to keep duplicates and order, toSet for distinctness, joining for a string, counting for a tally. Swapping toSet for toList would keep every city including repeats, so the choice of the innermost collector expresses the business rule directly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India plans regional training and needs to know, for each department, the distinct cities where its staff are based, so it can book venues. Priya does not need every employee, and she does not want the same city listed twice if several colleagues share it — she needs the unique set of cities per department.

This is exactly what groupingBy with a mapping-to-Set downstream produces — it groups by department, pulls out just the city from each employee, and collapses duplicates into a distinct set.

The code defines `Employee`, a `TrainingPlannerService.citiesByDepartment` method, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: five employees; Trading has Rajesh and Rohit both in Mumbai plus Sneha in Bangalore; Risk has Priya in Mumbai and Neha in Pune.

Step 1: The classifier groups by department, forming Trading and Risk buckets.

Step 2: For each employee the mapping extracts just the city, discarding the rest of the object.

Step 3: Within the Trading bucket, toSet receives Mumbai, Bangalore, and Mumbai again; the duplicate Mumbai collapses, leaving Mumbai and Bangalore.

Step 4: Within the Risk bucket, toSet receives Mumbai and Pune, both kept.

Step 5: The result is a map of department to a distinct set of cities, ready for venue planning.

```
INFO: Trading -> [Mumbai, Bangalore]
INFO: Risk -> [Mumbai, Pune]
```

```

    │ groupingBy(department)
    ├─ Trading: [Rajesh/Mumbai, Sneha/Bangalore, Rohit/Mumbai]
    │     mapping(getCity) → Mumbai, Bangalore, Mumbai
    │     toSet() → {Mumbai, Bangalore}   (dup collapsed)
    └─ Risk: [Priya/Mumbai, Neha/Pune]
          mapping(getCity) → Mumbai, Pune
          toSet() → {Mumbai, Pune}
    ▼
  Map<String, Set<String>>
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The mapping collector transforms each element before it reaches a downstream collector, and it becomes powerful when nested inside groupingBy. By writing groupingBy of department with a downstream of mapping of get city into toSet, I group employees by department and, within each group, keep only the distinct cities rather than the whole employee objects. The toSet collapses duplicate cities so each appears once per department.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India we planned regional training and needed, for each department, the unique set of cities where its staff were based so we could book venues. If two Trading colleagues were both in Mumbai I did not want Mumbai listed twice, and the mapping-to-Set downstream gave me exactly the distinct cities per department in one collect call.

The senior point I always make is that collectors compose like building blocks, and each block expresses part of the business rule. The classifier chooses the key, mapping chooses what the grouped values are, and the innermost collector chooses how they are gathered — toSet for distinctness, toList to keep duplicates and order, counting for a tally, joining for a string. Changing just the innermost collector changes the business meaning without touching the grouping logic.
